definition: Fetid means giving off a strong, foul smell.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fetid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fetid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A fetid haze hung over the flooded crawl space, where a month of standing water had steeped in the dark.
Stuffy air is merely close and unrefreshed — it wants an open window, nothing worse — and it sits far below fetid, where the stillness itself has gone foul.
Suffocating goes further than fetid — fetid air revolts the people breathing it; suffocating air can barely be breathed at all.

Reeking says a strong smell is actively pouring off something — and it can be any smell at all, even perfume or gasoline. Fetid is narrower and darker: the foulness of shut-in air and standing water, stale places gone rotten. A locker room reeks; a sealed cellar is fetid.

Stinking is the plain, everyday word for smelling bad, at home anywhere from a gym bag to a garbage truck. Fetid adds the shut-in, unmoving note — air or water that has stood in the dark until the stillness itself turned foul.

Latin fetere, "to stink," left almost nothing else behind in English — only fetor, a term physicians use for a diagnostic odor, and that is this word's own close kin rather than a new relative. The memory hook is the suffix instead: -id words name standing states, and fetid names the state of stinking.
Fetid means giving off a strong, foul smell.
The courthouse cistern had been sealed since the fifties, and the surveyor who finally cracked the hatch reeled back off the ladder.
Below him lay sixty years of trapped water — black, still, skinned with scum — and fetid air that had been breathing only itself since Eisenhower.
He taped the hatch open and gave it two days before anyone went down.

Fetid is the exact word for that air, because it means giving off a strong, foul smell — and the word leans hard toward staleness gone rotten: shut-in rooms, standing water, spaces the wind never rinses.
Musty is the closet's mild complaint; stuffy is merely unrefreshed.
Fetid says the stillness itself has gone foul.
Fetid is for airless, standing places — trapped air, still water, rooms the wind never reaches.

Its unit-mates split the territory: putrid is the smell of flesh and food actively decaying, rancid belongs to fats and oils gone over, and noisome is the broadest — offensive or outright harmful, smelly or not.
If the scene is a swamp, a bilge, or a sealed basement, fetid is your word.
